title: Reliability Patterns
description: Build systems that stay available under stress. Master SLA, SLO, and SLI definitions; circuit breakers, bulkheads, retries, timeouts, and graceful degradation; and how to measure and improve reliability systematically.

data.text: Reliability is not the absence of failures. It is the ability to recover from them quickly and gracefully. Senior engineers design for failure because they know that in large distributed systems, something is always breaking somewhere.
Reliability patterns are reusable tactics that make systems resilient. Used together, they form a safety net that protects users and the business from cascading failures.

An SLA (Service Level Agreement) is a promise to customers about performance. An SLO (Service Level Objective) is the internal target that makes the SLA achievable. An SLI (Service Level Indicator) is the actual measured metric.

rows: HTTP request latency, error rate, throughput
The target value for the SLI
If uptime drops below 99.9%, customers receive a credit

data.text: A circuit breaker prevents a failing service from being called repeatedly. It works like an electrical circuit breaker: when failures exceed a threshold, the breaker trips and stops all calls for a cooldown period. This gives the failing service time to recover and prevents resource exhaustion in the caller.

data.title: Circuit Breaker States
items: Closed: requests flow normally; failures are counted
Open: requests fail immediately without calling the downstream service
Half-Open: after a timeout, a limited number of test requests are allowed through to check recovery

data.text: Bulkheading isolates failures by limiting the resources that a single failure can consume. Think of ship bulkheads: if one compartment floods, the others stay dry. In software, you might use separate thread pools, connection pools, or queues for different operations.

Retries handle transient failures — network blips, temporary overloads, or brief service unavailability. Always retry with exponential backoff and a maximum attempt count. Retrying too aggressively can make an overloaded service worse.

data.title: Exponential Backoff Formula
data.code:
Attempt 1: 1s   (base 1s, 2^0)
Attempt 2: 2s   (1s × 2^1)
Attempt 3: 4s   (1s × 2^2)
Attempt 4: 8s   (1s × 2^3)
Max attempts: 5
Jitter: ±10% random variation to prevent thundering herd

data.text: Every external call should have a timeout. Without one, a slow downstream service can exhaust your connection pool and take down the entire system. Set timeouts at every layer: HTTP client, database query, and message queue.

Graceful degradation means the system continues to function, albeit in a reduced mode, when a component fails. If the recommendation engine is down, show popular products instead of showing an error page.

data.title: Reliability Principle
data.text: Design for failure in production, not in testing. Chaos engineering — deliberately injecting failures in production-like environments — is how leading companies prove their reliability patterns work before real outages happen.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: SLOs translate business promises into measurable engineering targets
Circuit breakers stop cascading failures by isolating failing services
Bulkheads contain failures to prevent resource exhaustion
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter for transient failures only
Timeouts at every layer protect your system from slow dependencies
Graceful degradation keeps the system usable when parts fail
data.takeaway: Reliability is engineered, not assumed. Build patterns into your architecture from day one.

items.question: What is a reasonable SLO for a web application?
items.answer: Most consumer-facing applications target 99.9% availability (about 8.7 hours of downtime per year). For critical financial or health systems, 99.99% (52 minutes per year) is more appropriate.

items.question: Should I retry all failed requests?
items.answer: No. Retry only idempotent or safe operations. Never retry a payment POST without an idempotency key. Retrying non-idempotent writes can create duplicates or double charges.

items.question: How do I know if my circuit breaker is working?
items.answer: Monitor the circuit state transitions. If the breaker is constantly tripping, the downstream service has a real problem that needs fixing — not just a transient glitch.

data.title: Design a Resilient Payment Gateway
data.description: Your application calls an external payment gateway that occasionally times out. Design a resilient client using circuit breaker, retry with exponential backoff, timeout, and fallback. Specify thresholds, timeouts, and what the fallback does when the gateway is unavailable.
data.expectedOutcome: A design document or code sketch showing circuit breaker thresholds, retry policy, timeout values, and a fallback strategy (such as queuing for later processing).
